title: How a Telephone Turns Your Voice into Electricity
summary: When you talk, you make the air wiggle. A telephone catches those wiggles with a thin, shaky disk and turns them into a wiggling electric current, then a magnet at the other end shakes another disk to make your voice again. Inventors like Thomas Edison made phones much louder by squeezing tiny grains of carbon, and Edison even helped make 'Hello!' the word we say when we pick up.

sections.heading: Sound Is a Shove in the Air
paragraphs: Put your fingers gently on the front of your throat and hum. Feel that buzzing? That is your vocal cords, two small folds of tissue in your voice box, snapping open and shut hundreds of times every second. Each time they flap, they give the air coming up from your lungs a tiny shove. That shove pushes on the air in front of your mouth, which pushes on the air in front of it, and so on, like a long line of people bumping shoulders in a crowded hallway.

This travelling pattern of squeezes and stretches is what scientists call a sound wave. Where the air molecules are pushed close together, the pressure is a little higher. Where they spread apart, the pressure is a little lower. The air itself does not fly across the room from your mouth to your friend's ear. Instead, each little bit of air jiggles back and forth and passes the push along, the way a wave travels across a stadium while every fan stays in their seat.

How fast does the wave move? In air at room temperature, sound travels about 343 metres (about 1,125 feet) every second. NASA's guide for students gives a slightly lower figure, about 1,100 feet per second, for the colder standard air used in aircraft calculations, because sound moves a little faster when air is warmer. Either way, that is quick enough that a friend across a classroom hears you almost instantly, but slow enough that you see a lightning flash before you hear the thunder.

When the wave reaches your friend, it bumps into their eardrum, a thin, tight piece of skin deep inside the ear. The eardrum is pushed in when the pressure rises and pulled out when it drops, so it copies the shape of the sound wave exactly. Three tiny bones behind it pass the motion on, and nerves turn it into signals the brain understands as words, music or the barking of a dog.

Two features of the wave matter most. The first is how many times per second it vibrates, called its frequency and measured in hertz. A low voice might vibrate around 100 times a second, a high whistle several thousand. A healthy young ear can hear from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz. The second feature is how big the pushes are, called the amplitude. Big pushes sound loud; small pushes sound quiet.

Here is the important part. A spoken word is not one neat, single vibration. The sound of 'ahh' and the sound of 'eee' have different mixtures of frequencies stacked on top of each other, and consonants like 's' and 't' are quick hisses and pops. That is why speech is so tricky to send. A telegraph only had to say 'on' or 'off'. A telephone had to copy a messy, constantly changing wave, with all its wiggles in the right places, and rebuild it somewhere else.

sections.heading: Copying the Shape of a Voice
paragraphs: Alexander Graham Bell's great insight, the one he chased after the twanging reed of June 1875, was that you did not need to turn speech into a code at all. You could make an electric current that rose and fell in exactly the same pattern as the air pressure of the voice. Bell called this an 'undulating' current, meaning a current that moves up and down in waves. If the current copied the wave faithfully, the far end only had to turn it back into motion.

The part of a telephone that does the copying is called the transmitter, the piece you speak into. At its heart sits a diaphragm, a thin, flexible disk, usually of metal. When the sound wave from your mouth reaches it, the diaphragm is pushed in and out just as your eardrum would be. In a sense, the transmitter is an electric ear. Its job is to make the current flowing through it change every time the diaphragm moves.

Bell tried two main ways of doing this. In the first, used for the famous 'Mr. Watson' call on March 10, 1876, a needle attached to the diaphragm dipped into a small cup of water mixed with acid. As the diaphragm moved, the needle went a little deeper or a little shallower. Electricity passes through the acid water more easily when there is less water to cross, so the current rose and fell with the voice. It worked, but sloshing acid was hardly practical for a phone in someone's kitchen.

The second method, which Bell used in his public demonstrations and in the first telephones sold to customers, needed no battery at all. A thin iron diaphragm sat just in front of a magnet wrapped in a coil of wire. When your voice moved the iron disk, it disturbed the magnet's invisible field, and that changing magnetism pushed a tiny current through the coil. This is the same principle of induction that Michael Faraday had discovered back in 1831. Your voice itself was making the electricity.

Either way, the result was what engineers call an analog signal. Analog means that the signal is a smooth copy, an 'analogy', of something else. If you could draw a graph of the air pressure in front of your mouth and another graph of the current in the wire, the two curves would have the same shape. A rise in pressure became a rise in current; a quick wiggle in the sound became a quick wiggle in the electricity. Nothing was turned into numbers. The current simply mirrored the wave, like a shadow follows the hand that makes it.

Once the signal is electric, distance stops being about the speed of sound. Electrical signals in a wire move at a large fraction of the speed of light, hundreds of thousands of kilometres every second. Shout across a valley and your voice takes several seconds to reach the far side and echo back. Send it down a wire and, for a listener a town away, the delay is far too small for any human to notice. The voice is still yours, but it is riding on electricity instead of air.

sections.heading: The Earpiece: A Magnet That Talks
paragraphs: At the other end of the line, the listener needs the opposite of a microphone: a device that turns a changing current back into moving air. This is the receiver, the earpiece. If the transmitter is an electric ear, the receiver is an electric mouth.

A classic receiver has three main parts. There is a permanent magnet, the ordinary kind that always attracts iron. Around one end of it, or around an iron core near it, is a coil of fine insulated wire. And in front of the magnet, almost but not quite touching it, sits another thin iron diaphragm. The permanent magnet holds the diaphragm under a gentle, steady pull, bending it very slightly toward the magnet.

Now send the voice current through the coil. A coil carrying current becomes an electromagnet, and its strength depends on how much current is flowing. When the current from the line rises, the coil adds to the permanent magnet's pull and the diaphragm is tugged a little closer. When the current falls, the pull weakens and the springy diaphragm moves back out. Because the current is a copy of the speaker's sound wave, the diaphragm now moves in the same pattern as the speaker's diaphragm did. It pushes and pulls on the air beside your ear, and the sound wave is born again.

Why bother with the permanent magnet? Without it, an iron diaphragm would be attracted whether the current flowed one way or the other, so it would vibrate twice as often as it should and the voice would come out garbled. The steady magnet gives the diaphragm a resting position to swing either side of, so a rise in current pulls it in and a dip lets it out. That simple trick keeps the copy honest.

Bell's electromagnetic receiver was such a good design that its basic idea lasted for a very long time. The very first telephones Bell's company rented out were simple wooden or hard-rubber tubes containing a magnet, a coil and a diaphragm. People sometimes call the 1877 to 1878 handheld version the 'butterstamp' telephone because its turned wooden handle looked like a tool for pressing patterns into butter. The same instrument served as both transmitter and receiver: you talked into it, then quickly moved it to your ear to listen. Some users had two, one for the mouth and one for the ear.

Look inside an old landline handset from the twentieth century and you will still find a magnet, a coil and a diaphragm in the earpiece. Even the little speakers in modern earbuds work on a related idea, using a coil and a magnet to move a thin membrane. When you listen to music, you are using a great-great-grandchild of the receiver Bell and Thomas Watson were building in a Boston workshop.

Later telephone designers added a thoughtful touch. When you speak into a landline handset, a little of your own voice is deliberately fed back into your own earpiece. Engineers call this 'sidetone'. Without it, the phone feels strangely dead, as if you were talking into a pillow, and people tend to raise their voices until they are shouting. With just the right amount, you hear yourself naturally and speak at a comfortable volume. It is a small example of how the science of the telephone is also the science of how humans listen.

sections.heading: The Problem of the Whispering Wire
paragraphs: Bell's magnet telephone had one big weakness, and anyone who used it noticed straight away: it was quiet. Very quiet. Early users often had to press the instrument hard against one ear, cover the other ear with a hand, and ask the speaker to talk loudly and slowly. Over a short line it was a marvel. Over a long one, the voice faded to a whisper buried in crackles.

The reason comes straight from the physics. In Bell's magnet transmitter, all the electrical energy on the line came from the speaker's voice. A voice carries surprisingly little energy. The gentle pushes of air that move a diaphragm can only create a feeble current in a coil, and that feeble current then has to travel through kilometres of wire, which resists it and wastes some of it as heat. By the time it arrived, there was not much left to shake the listener's diaphragm.

Think of it like this. Imagine trying to ring a big church bell at the far end of a long rope by blowing on your end of the rope. However cleverly you blow, there simply is not enough push. What you really want is a strong motor at your end of the rope, and a way for your breath to control that motor. Then your gentle effort decides when and how the bell moves, while the motor supplies the muscle.

That is exactly the trick the next generation of transmitters used. Instead of the voice making the current, a battery made a strong, steady current, and the voice merely controlled how much of that current got through. The voice became like a hand on a tap, opening and closing it, while the battery was the water pressure in the pipes. A small movement of the hand could make a big change in the flow.

This difference sounds small, but it changed everything about how far a call could go. With a magnet transmitter, a louder phone meant shouting harder, and there is a limit to how loudly anyone can shout. With a battery-powered transmitter, engineers could choose a stronger battery or a better circuit, and every word would arrive with more strength behind it. The question was no longer 'How hard can a person talk?' but 'How sensitive can we make the tap?'

Several inventors had already noticed a useful fact about electrical contacts. When two pieces of a conducting material just barely touch, the electrical resistance between them, how hard it is for current to pass, depends strongly on how firmly they are pressed together. Press harder and more tiny points touch, so current flows more easily. Press more lightly and the current is choked down. In Germany, Johann Philipp Reis had used loose contacts in his Telephon back in 1861. Now, in the late 1870s, inventors on both sides of the Atlantic turned to one particular material that was very good at this: carbon.

sections.heading: Three Inventors and a Pinch of Soot
paragraphs: Imagine a long wooden laboratory building in Menlo Park, New Jersey, in 1877, crammed with jars, wires and batteries, with lamps burning late into the night. This was the workshop of Thomas Alva Edison, already famous for his telegraph inventions. Western Union, the giant telegraph company, was paying him to improve on Bell's telephone, and Edison set his team testing material after material to find the best one for a pressure-sensitive contact.

Edison, who was himself hard of hearing, tried many substances. The winner turned out to be carbon in very fine form, including lampblack, the dark soot collected from smoky oil lamps, pressed into a small, firm button. Placed behind the diaphragm, the carbon button was squeezed a tiny bit harder whenever the voice pushed the diaphragm in, and relaxed whenever it moved out. Its resistance rose and fell with the voice, so the strong current from a battery rose and fell too. The result was a voice much louder and clearer than Bell's magnet transmitter could manage. Edison's carbon transmitter took shape between 1877 and 1878, and his patents covered several versions of it.

Edison was not alone. In the United States, a young German immigrant named Emile Berliner was working on the same problem in his spare time. Born in Hanover in 1851, Berliner had come to the United States in 1870 and studied physics in evening classes at Cooper Union in New York while doing odd jobs. In 1877 he worked out a loose-contact transmitter in which a metal diaphragm pressed against a contact point, so that changes in pressure changed the current. He also patented an induction coil for telephones, which we will meet again soon. The Bell company was impressed enough to acquire his patent, and Berliner went to work for it, leaving in 1883 to research on his own. He later became even more famous for the flat-disc gramophone record.

Across the ocean in London, the inventor and former music professor David Edward Hughes was exploring loose contacts with almost childlike simplicity. In one experiment he laid an ordinary iron nail across two other nails connected to a battery and a telephone receiver. The wobbly contact was so sensitive that tiny sounds near it, even faint scratches, were picked up and heard in the receiver. He refined the idea using small pencils of carbon held loosely between carbon blocks. His paper on it was read to the Royal Society in London on May 8, 1878.

Hughes gave the device the name we still use: the microphone, borrowing a word that Charles Wheatstone had used decades earlier for a sound-amplifying gadget. Even more remarkably, Hughes chose not to patent it. He believed the discovery should be free for everyone to develop. Many historians give Hughes much credit for working out how loose-contact carbon microphones really behave.

So who invented the carbon microphone? As so often in this story, the fair answer is that several people reached similar ideas at almost the same time. Edison and Berliner fought a long legal battle over American patent rights, and in 1901 a United States appeals court ruled Berliner's patent invalid and sided with Edison, stating that the use of carbon in a transmitter was Edison's invention. Hughes, who had stayed out of the patent race, kept his scientific reputation and later received the Royal Society's Royal Medal. Each man added something real.

sections.heading: A Hundred Years of Carbon Grains
paragraphs: The carbon idea kept improving. Around 1878–79 Francis Blake, working with the Bell company, developed a transmitter in which a platinum contact pressed against a hard carbon button, and the 'Blake transmitter' became the standard Bell mouthpiece for many years. Around the same time, the English inventor Henry Hunnings patented a transmitter filled with loose carbon granules, tiny grains a bit like coarse black sand, instead of one solid button. Lots of grains meant lots of contact points, and lots of contact points made the transmitter more sensitive.

In 1892, a Bell engineer named Anthony C. White patented the 'solid-back' transmitter. It held the carbon granules in a small, sealed chamber between a fixed carbon disk at the back and a carbon disk attached to the diaphragm at the front. This design was tough, loud and reliable, and versions of it were used for decades. Its descendants were the carbon transmitters screwed into the mouthpieces of telephones well into the late twentieth century.

To understand why the grains worked so well, imagine a jar of marbles. Push on the lid and the marbles squash together, touching each other at more places and with more force. Carbon granules behave the same way, but electrically. When a sound wave presses the diaphragm in, the grains are squeezed, they touch more firmly, the resistance drops and more current flows. When the pressure eases, the grains loosen, the resistance rises and less current flows. Squeezed harder means more current; squeezed less means less current. The current dances to the rhythm of your voice.

There was one more clever helper: the induction coil. A telephone line is long and resists current, so engineers added a small transformer, two coils of wire wound around an iron core, to each telephone set. The transmitter's changing current flowed through the first coil, and the second coil, with many more turns of wire, produced a matching signal at a higher voltage that travelled more efficiently along the line. Berliner and Edison both worked on this idea, and it became a standard part of the telephone.

Put together, carbon granules, a battery and an induction coil turned the telephone from a whispering novelty into a practical tool. The carbon transmitter actually gave out more electrical energy than the voice put in, because the battery supplied the extra. In other words, it acted as an amplifier, something that makes a weak signal stronger. Early telephone engineers even built carbon-based amplifiers to boost signals on long lines before vacuum tubes came along.

The carbon microphone also had faults. It produced a faint hissing noise, it did not reproduce the highest and lowest sounds very faithfully, and the grains could pack together over time, especially if the phone sat unused. Old telephone users sometimes tapped the handset to loosen them. But for ordinary speech those faults did not matter much. The design was cheap, simple, sturdy and loud. Carbon-granule microphones remained standard in telephones from the 1880s until roughly the 1980s, when electronic microphones finally replaced them. For about a hundred years, almost every phone call in the world travelled through a pinch of carbon.

sections.heading: Hello, Hulloa or Ahoy?
paragraphs: Once a voice could leap down a wire, people faced a surprisingly tricky question: what do you say first? Before the telephone, greetings usually happened face to face, where you could see who you were talking to and often said something linked to the time of day, like 'good morning'. On a phone line you could not see anyone, and you needed to grab the other person's attention before saying anything important.

Alexander Graham Bell had a favourite answer: 'Ahoy!' It was a sailor's call used to hail another ship across the water, and it fitted his picture of a voice calling out across a distance. Bell reportedly kept using it, but it never caught on with the public.

Thomas Edison suggested something different. In a letter dated August 15, 1877, to T. B. A. David, the president of a telegraph company in Pittsburgh, Edison proposed shouting 'Hello!' into the instrument. He argued that the word could be heard 10 to 20 feet (about 3 to 6 metres) away, so it could even do the job of a bell, telling someone across the room that a call was coming. 'Hello' and similar words like 'hullo' and 'halloo' already existed as ways of calling out to someone or showing surprise, but Edison's suggestion helped make it the telephone word.

Hello spread with the telephone itself. Telephone companies and operators used it, and by the late 1880s operators at telephone exchanges were being nicknamed 'hello girls'. Within a generation, picking up a phone and saying 'Hello?' felt so natural that people began to forget it had ever been a choice. You may hear a story that 'hello' was named after a woman connected to Bell. That is a myth with no evidence behind it; the word was around long before.

So the next time you answer a call, you are taking part in a small piece of history: a little contest between two great inventors, which Edison won. Bell's 'Ahoy!' lives on mostly in pirate films and on boats.

But notice something about this chapter. Edison was improving the telephone while working for Western Union, Bell's biggest rival. Berliner's patent was bought by the Bell company. Hughes gave his discovery away. Every improvement made the telephone more valuable, and the more valuable it became, the more people wanted a share of it. Better phones were about to lead to bigger fights: over patents, over money, and over the most explosive question of all, who had really invented the telephone in the first place.

deepDive: Engineers describe a telephone as a pair of transducers, devices that change energy from one form to another: the transmitter turns acoustic energy into electrical energy and the receiver does the reverse. Bell's first commercial instruments used the same electromagnetic transducer at both ends. Because induction produces a voltage proportional to how fast the magnetic field changes, the energy available was tiny, and every kilometre of line, with its resistance and capacitance, drained and blurred the signal further. The carbon transmitter changed the energy budget completely. It is not a generator but a variable resistor in a battery circuit, so the power delivered to the line comes from the battery, while the voice only modulates it. That makes it an amplifying transducer, with a power gain greater than one, decades before vacuum-tube amplifiers. The physics of why loose carbon contacts work so well is more subtle than 'squeezing increases contact area'. Hughes argued in 1878 that the effect came from the many microscopic points where carbon pieces touch rather than from compressing the carbon itself; modern explanations add that the number and size of these tiny contact spots, and thin surface films on them, change with pressure. Carbon was attractive because it conducts electricity, does not rust or easily weld together under sparking, and stays fairly stable over time. Its drawbacks were noise, non-linear response (louder sounds were not reproduced in exact proportion), a limited frequency range and 'packing' of granules. For speech these were acceptable, since intelligibility depends mainly on frequencies roughly between a few hundred and a few thousand hertz, the band later standardised for telephone networks. Credit for the carbon microphone remains genuinely shared: Edison won the decisive American patent rulings, ending with a 1901 appeals court decision against Berliner's patent; Hughes published openly in Britain and never patented; Berliner, Blake, Hunnings and White all contributed practical improvements. The story is a good example of how a key component is often the result of many overlapping efforts rather than a single flash of genius.
funFact: In an August 1877 letter, Thomas Edison recommended answering the telephone with 'Hello!' because, he said, it could be heard 10 to 20 feet away, while Alexander Graham Bell preferred to say 'Ahoy!'

check.q: In a carbon transmitter, what happens when sound pushes the diaphragm in and squeezes the carbon grains?
check.a: The grains touch more firmly, their resistance drops and more current flows
wrong: The grains catch fire and make a spark that carries the voice
The grains become magnetic and pull on the wire
The current stops completely until the diaphragm moves back
